vignette:
**Patient Vignette: Dr. M., Age 40, Surgeon**

Dr. M. is a tall, precise man who speaks in measured sentences, as if he is still dictating post-operative notes. He sits with his hands clasped, his wedding ring catching the light. He has been married for twelve years, has two young children, and is a respected cardiothoracic surgeon. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, after she found him standing in their dark kitchen at 3 a.m., unable to speak.

He tells the story of the earthquake in a flat, clinical tone. It happened eighteen months ago, during a humanitarian mission in a coastal region. He was in a temporary surgical tent when the ground began to move. He remembers the sound first—a deep, grinding roar that seemed to come from inside his own chest. The tent collapsed. The lights went out. He was pinned beneath a steel beam for nearly four hours.

“I was conscious the whole time,” he says, his eyes fixed on a point on the wall. “I could hear people screaming. I could feel the beam on my legs. I could smell the dust and the blood. I knew the building above me was unstable. I calculated the probability of another collapse. It was high.”

He was rescued by a local team. He had a fractured tibia and three broken ribs. He was evacuated, flown home, and spent six weeks in physical recovery. He returned to work eight weeks after the accident. The hospital praised his resilience. He told no one about the nightmares.

But the nightmares came anyway. In them, he is always in the tent. The beam is heavier. The screaming is louder. Sometimes, he is not the victim but the surgeon, trying to operate on himself while the ground shakes. He wakes with his heart hammering, his sheets drenched, his hands numb. He has not had a full night’s sleep in over a year.

At work, he is a different man. His hands, once steady, now tremble slightly before the first incision. He double-checks his own work obsessively, sometimes three or four times. He has started arriving two hours early to review charts, because he cannot trust his memory. A colleague joked that he had become “too careful.” Dr. M. did not find it funny.

He avoids the hospital’s basement level. He takes the stairs instead of the elevator, because the enclosed space reminds him of being trapped. He has stopped attending the weekly surgical debriefs, where the fluorescent lights flicker. He tells himself it is a scheduling conflict.

At home, he is distant. His wife says he is “not there.” He sits at the dinner table but does not eat. He watches his children play but does not join them. He feels as though a pane of glass has been lowered between him and the rest of the world. He can see them, but he cannot reach them. He has not felt joy, or even anticipation, in months.

The most troubling symptom, he says, is the hypervigilance. He scans every room for exits. He flinches at sudden sounds—a dropped tray, a car horn, a door slamming. He has started checking the structural integrity of buildings. He notices cracks in walls, loose ceiling tiles, the weight of a chandelier. He cannot stop.

“I know it’s irrational,” he says, his voice barely above a whisper. “I know the hospital is safe. I know my home is safe. But my body does not know. My body is still in that tent.”

He pauses. His hands are shaking. He looks at me, and for the first time, his eyes are not clinical. They are tired.

“I used to be able to compartmentalize,” he says. “That’s what surgeons do. But this—this is not a compartment. It is everywhere.”
